claim: Arabidopsis seed germination is blocked in the vicinity of the plant pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: We found that Arabidopsis seed germination is blocked in the vicinity of the plant pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, where germination is strongly repressed by P. aeruginosa strains PAO1 and PA14.

claim: L-2-amino-4-methoxy-trans-3-butenoic acid (AMB) is released by P. aeruginosa and triggers germination arrest.
source: We identified L-2-amino-4-methoxy-trans-3-butenoic acid (AMB), released by P. aeruginosa, as a biotic compound triggering germination arrest.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomic analysis and biochemical purification procedures described in the manuscript, as well as germination assays with synthetic AMB shown in Figure 4.

claim: In AMB-treated seeds, DELLA factors promote the accumulation of the germination repressor ABI5 in a GA-independent manner.
source: We provide genetic evidence that in AMB-treated seeds DELLA factors promote the accumulation of the germination repressor ABI5 in a GA-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6, including protein gel blot analysis and transcriptome analysis.

claim: AMB production is controlled by the quorum sensing system IQS.
source: AMB production is controlled by the quorum sensing system IQS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with P. aeruginosa mutant strains deficient in the AMB operon (ΔambE) shown in Figure 4, and by citation of previous work by Lee et al. (2013a).

claim: The AMB-dependent germination arrest protects seedlings from damage induced by AMB.
source: In vitro experiments show that the AMB-dependent germination arrest protects seedlings from damage induced by AMB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 7, where germination-arrested seeds produce viable plants when no longer exposed to AMB or P. aeruginosa, while seedlings that germinated in the presence of AMB show severe developmental defects.

claim: Germination was not markedly repressed by P. fluorescens, P. putida, P. syringae or Escherichia coli.
source: Germination was not markedly repressed by P. fluorescens, P. putida, P. syringae or Escherichia coli (used as a Gram-negative non-Pseudomonas species control) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Germination was strongly repressed by P. aeruginosa (WT strains PAO1 and PA14).
source: In marked contrast, germination was strongly repressed by P. aeruginosa (WT strains PAO1 and PA14) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The percentage of germination increased with increasing distance separating seeds and P. aeruginosa.
source: The percentage of germination increased with increasing distance separating seeds and P. aeruginosa (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Germination arrest did not occur in absence of germination medium separating bacteria and seeds.
source: Furthermore, germination arrest did not occur in absence of germination medium separating bacteria and seeds (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P. aeruginosa releases a germination repressive activity (GRA) that diffuses in the germination medium.
source: From these observations, we conclude that P. aeruginosa releases a germination repressive activity (GRA) that diffuses in the germination medium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations that germination arrest depends on distance from bacteria and requires germination medium.

claim: Upon imbibition seeds respond to unfavorable abiotic conditions by blocking GA synthesis, which promotes DELLA factors accumulation.
source: Upon imbibition seeds respond to unfavorable abiotic conditions by blocking GA synthesis, which promotes DELLA factors accumulation.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about seed germination control.

claim: DELLA factors collectively repress seed germination by stimulating ABA signaling including the accumulation of the germination repressor TF ABI5.
source: In turn, DELLA factors collectively repress seed germination by stimulating ABA signaling including the accumulation of the germination repressor TF ABI5 (Piskurewicz et al., 2008, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Piskurewicz et al. (2008, 2009).

claim: GA signaling mutant seeds, lacking one or several DELLA factors, had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of WT P. aeruginosa (PAO1).
source: GA signaling mutant seeds, lacking one or several DELLA factors and particularly ∆della mutant seeds lacking all five DELLA factors, had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of WT P. aeruginosa (PAO1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Arabidopsis mutant seeds deficient in ABA synthesis (aba1) or signaling (abi3, abi5) had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of P. aeruginosa (PAO1).
source: Furthermore, Arabidopsis mutant seeds deficient in ABA synthesis (aba1) or signaling (abi3, abi5) also had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of P. aeruginosa (PAO1) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa (PAO1) persistently accumulated RGL2 and ABI5 up to 148 hr upon imbibition, which was associated with low germination percentage.
source: However, WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa (PAO1) persistently accumulated RGL2 and ABI5 up to 148 hr upon imbibition, which was associated with low germination percentage (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ∆della mutant seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts did not maintain ABI5 accumulation over time upon imbibition, which was associated with increasing germination percentage.
source: In contrast, ∆della mutant seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts did not maintain ABI5 accumulation over time upon imbibition, which was associated with increasing germination percentage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The GRA released by P. aeruginosa represses germination by promoting DELLA-dependent increase of the germination repressor ABI5.
source: These observations indicate that the GRA released by P. aeruginosa represses germination by promoting DELLA-dependent increase of the germination repressor ABI5, as previously shown with seeds unable to synthesize GA upon imbibition (Piskurewicz et al., 2008, 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by citation of previous work.

claim: Exogenous GA (10 µM) did not promote germination of WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts.
source: However, and surprisingly, exogenous GA (10 µM) did not promote germination of WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts and exogenous GA showed persistent accumulation of RGL2 and ABI5.
source: This was associated with persistent accumulation of RGL2 and ABI5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exogenous GA promoted the germination of WT seeds exposed to paclobutrazol (PAC), an inhibitor of GA synthesis.
source: In contrast, and expectedly, exogenous GA promoted the germination of WT seeds exposed to paclobutrazol (PAC), an inhibitor of GA synthesis, which was associated with downregulation of RGL2 and ABI5 protein levels, consistent with previous results (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5B.

claim: The GRA could elicit a DELLA-dependent germination arrest irrespective of GA levels in seeds.
source: Thus, the GRA could elicit a DELLA-dependent germination arrest irrespective of GA levels in seeds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that exogenous GA does not rescue germination in seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts.

claim: AMB does not interfere with GA synthesis.
source: Our results strongly suggest that AMB does not interfere with GA synthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations that exogenous GA does not rescue germination and that AMB does not prevent GA-dependent DELLA degradation.

claim: AMB can regulate seed gene expression in both a DELLA-dependent and GA-independent manner.
source: Rather, they suggest that AMB can regulate seed gene expression in both a DELLA-dependent and GA-independent manner (Figure 3 and 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3 and protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AMB does not interfere with GA-dependent DELLA degradation.
source: Our results with RGL2, GAI and RGA suggest that AMB does not interfere with GA-dependent DELLA degradation (Figures 4B,6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figures 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of as many as 1103 genes was changed in PAC-treated WT seeds relative to untreated WT seeds.
source: The expression of as many as 1103 genes was changed in PAC-treated WT seeds relative to untreated WT seeds (MS vs PAC, Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Only three genes had their expression affected in PAC-treated Δdella seeds relative to untreated Δdella seeds.
source: In contrast, only three genes had their expression affected in PAC-treated Δdella seeds relative to untreated Δdella seeds (MS vs PAC, Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: DELLA factors influence gene expression mainly when GA synthesis is compromised.
source: Thus, DELLA factors influence gene expression mainly when GA synthesis is compromised, consistent with previous reports (Cao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq data and supported by citation of previous work by Cao et al. (2006).

claim: Only 130 genes had their expression changed in WT seeds exposed to PAO1 extract relative to non-exposed WT seeds.
source: In contrast to PAC-treated WT seeds, only 130 genes had their expression changed in WT seeds exposed to PAO1 extract relative to non-exposed WT seeds (MS vs PAO1 extract, Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Among the 130 genes, the expression of 87 genes was DELLA-dependent since it did not change in Δdella seeds exposed to PAO1 extract.
source: Among the 130 genes, the expression of 87 genes was DELLA-dependent since it did not change in Δdella seeds exposed to PAO1 extract (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: About a quarter of the 87 genes (24 genes) had their expression unchanged when GA was included in the medium together with PAO1 extract.
source: Strikingly, about a quarter of the 87 genes (24 genes) had their expression unchanged when GA was included in the medium together with PAO1 extract (MS vs PAO1 extract +GA, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The GRA released by P. aeruginosa is able to elicit gene expression responses in a DELLA-dependent and GA-independent manner.
source: Altogether, these results show that the GRA released by P. aeruginosa is able to elicit gene expression responses in a DELLA-dependent and GA-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq analysis results.

claim: Markedly lower GRAs were released by ΔlasIΔrhlI and particularly with ΔambE mutants.
source: We observed markedly lower GRAs released by ΔlasIΔrhlI and particularly with ΔambE mutants (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lower GRAs were also observed with ΔambA-D mutants, each affected in individual AMB operon genes.
source: Lower GRAs were also observed with ΔambA-D mutants, each affected in individual AMB operon genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transgenic WT P. aeruginosa bacteria overexpressing the AMB operon (AMBox) released a higher GRA relative to the parental PAO1 line.
source: Furthermore, and strikingly, transgenic WT P. aeruginosa bacteria overexpressing the AMB operon (AMBox) released a higher GRA relative to the parental PAO1 line (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GRA released by P. aeruginosa is dependent on QS activity and particularly that of IQS.
source: Altogether, these results show that the GRA released by P. aeruginosa is dependent on QS activity and particularly that of IQS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations with QS mutants.

claim: P. aeruginosa is the only Pseudomonas species used in this study having the IQS QS.
source: The importance of IQS is further suggested by the fact that P. aeruginosa is the only Pseudomonas species used in this study having the IQS QS (Figure 1A) (Rojas Murcia et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation of previous work by Rojas Murcia et al. (2015) and Lee et al. (2013b).

claim: The top discriminant feature in metabolomic analysis was the mass spectrometry signal corresponding to oxyvinylglycine L-2-amino-4-methoxy-trans-3-butenoic acid (AMB).
source: The top discriminant feature was the mass spectrometry signal corresponding to oxyvinylglycine L-2-amino-4-methoxy-trans-3-butenoic acid (also referred as methoxyvinylglycine or AMB) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claim: Chromatographic methods led to the identification of a GRA present in a polar fraction of WT PAO1 and AMBox extracts but absent in that of ∆ambE extracts.
source: We next used chromatographic methods to fractionate WT PAO1, AMBox and ∆ambE extracts, which led to the identification of a GRA present in a polar fraction of WT PAO1 and AMBox extracts but absent in that of ∆ambE extracts (Materials and methods, Figure 4—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical purification procedures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Further fractionation of AMBox extracts led to the isolation of a purified fraction containing AMB and the GRA.
source: AMBox extracts were used to further fractionate the GRA-containing polar fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 6B). This led to the isolation of a purified fraction containing AMB (as confirmed by NMR) (Figure 4—figure supplement 6B, Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2) and the GRA (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical purification procedures and NMR analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6B, Figure 4—figure supplement 7, and Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2.

claim: Synthetic AMB dose response confirmed that AMB inhibits WT seed germination.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis synthetic AMB dose response for germination inhibition confirmed that AMB inhibits WT seed germination (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutant seeds deficient in GA signaling (∆della), ABA biosynthesis (aba1) or ABA signaling (abi3) had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of synthetic AMB.
source: Furthermore, mutant seeds deficient in GA signaling (∆della), ABA biosynthesis (aba1) or ABA signaling (abi3,) had a higher percentage of seed germination in presence of synthetic AMB (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A concentration of 50 μM synthetic AMB had a GRA equivalent to that 0.8 mg/ml PAO1 extract in germination plates.
source: A concentration of 50 μM synthetic AMB had a GRA equivalent to that 0.8 mg/ml PAO1 extract in germination plates (see dashed red line in Figure 4C E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: 0.8 mg/ml PAO1 extract provides only 16 μM of natural AMB.
source: However, we estimated that this extract concentration provides only 16 μM of natural AMB (quantification by targeted UHPLC-HRMS2 approach, Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The GRA of AMB-supplemented ∆ambE extract was similar to that present in PAO1 extracts.
source: The GRA of the AMB-supplemented ∆ambE extract was similar to that present in PAO1 extracts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ∆ambE extracts supplemented with AMBi or synthetic AMB contained the same GRA.
source: ∆ambE extracts supplemented with AMBi or synthetic AMB contained the same GRA (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: The GRA of synthetic AMB can be enhanced by the presence of other compounds present in P. aeruginosa extracts.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the GRA of synthetic AMB can be enhanced by the presence of other compounds present in P. aeruginosa extracts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discrepancy between the concentration of synthetic AMB and natural AMB needed to achieve equivalent GRA.

claim: As much as 200 μM of AVG did not noticeably repress Arabidopsis seed germination.
source: As much as 200 μM of AVG of did not noticeably repress Arabidopsis seed germination, consistent with previous reports, indicating that AMB is an oxyvinylglycine specifically repressing Arabidopsis seed germination (Figure 4—figure supplement 10) (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 10 and citation of previous work by Wilson et al. (2014).

claim: AVG is known to inhibit ethylene synthesis.
source: AVG is known to inhibit ethylene synthesis, suggesting that AMB does not block germination by inhibiting ethylene synthesis (further discussed below) (Adams and Yang, 1979; Huai et al., 2001; Capitani et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Adams and Yang (1979), Huai et al. (2001), and Capitani et al. (2002).

claim: WT seeds exposed to AMB persistently accumulated RGL2 and ABI5 over time, unlike unexposed seeds.
source: WT seeds exposed to AMB persistently accumulated RGL2 and ABI5 over time, unlike unexposed seeds (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Persistent high ABI5 accumulation was not observed in AMB-treated Δdella mutant seeds.
source: Persistent high ABI5 accumulation was not observed in AMB-treated Δdella mutant seeds (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Beyond 24 hr of imbibition in presence of AMB, PAC and GA, RGL2 protein levels persisted in seeds despite the presence of GA.
source: Furthermore, beyond 24 hr of imbibition in presence of AMB, PAC and GA, RGL2 protein levels persisted in seeds despite the presence of GA, unlike seeds treated with PAC and GA only (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AMB induces changes in RGL2 and ABI5 accumulation in a manner similar to that observed with P. aeruginosa or WT PAO1 extracts.
source: Thus, AMB induces changes in RGL2 and ABI5 accumulation in a manner similar to that observed with P. aeruginosa or WT PAO1 extracts (Figures 2C, D and 3B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of protein gel blot analyses shown in Figures 2C, D, 3B, and 5.

claim: AMB is the main GRA released by P. aeruginosa repressing germination in a DELLA- and ABA-signaling-dependent manner.
source: Altogether, these results conclusively show that AMB is the main GRA released by P. aeruginosa repressing germination in a DELLA- and ABA-signaling-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of metabolomic analysis, biochemical purification, and genetic experiments.

claim: No marked increase in RGL2, GAI and RGA protein levels was observed in presence of AMB or ABA despite the fact that both treatments arrested seed germination as in PAC-treated seeds.
source: In contrast, no marked increase in RGL2, GAI and RGA protein levels was observed in presence of AMB or ABA despite the fact that both treatments arrested seed germination as in PAC-treated seeds (Figure 6A, B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 6A, B and C.

claim: Upon addition of GA to the medium RGL2, RGA and GAI protein levels decreased over 28 hr in a similar manner to that observed in control plates lacking AMB.
source: Upon addition of GA to the medium RGL2, RGA and GAI protein levels decreased over 28 hr in a similar manner to that observed in control plates lacking AMB (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein gel blot analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: GA-dependent DELLA protein degradation is not affected in AMB-treated seeds.
source: Altogether, these results strongly suggest that GA-dependent DELLA protein degradation is not affected in AMB-treated seeds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the protein gel blot analyses showing that GA induces DELLA degradation in AMB-treated seeds.

claim: AMB-treated seeds accumulated markedly higher ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA levels relative to seeds imbibed in absence of AMB at 30 hr of imbibition.
source: Upon 30 hr of imbibition, seed accumulated the same RGL2 levels in absence (MS) or presence of AMB (AMB) (Figure 5A). Nevertheless, AMB-treated seeds accumulated markedly higher ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA levels relative to seeds imbibed in absence of AMB (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: AMB-treated Δdella mutant seeds accumulated lower ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA expression at 30 hr.
source: In contrast, AMB-treated Δdella mutant seeds accumulated lower ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA expression at 30 hr (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon 44 hr of imbibition, AMB-treated seeds further increased the expression of ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA as well as that of RGL2.
source: Upon 44 hr of imbibition, AMB-treated seeds further increased the expression of ABI5, EM1 and NCED6 mRNA as well as that of RGL2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The DELLA activity promoting ABA signaling in seeds is enhanced in AMB-treated seeds.
source: Collectively, these genetic observations support the notion that the DELLA activity promoting ABA signaling in seeds is enhanced in AMB-treated seeds (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic experiments showing increased ABA-responsive gene expression in AMB-treated seeds.

claim: AMB could still mildly stimulate EM1, NCED6 and particularly ABI5 mRNA expression in Δdella mutant seeds.
source: Interestingly, AMB could still mildly stimulate EM1, NCED6 and particularly ABI5 mRNA expression in Δdella mutant seeds (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A residual activity promoting ABA synthesis or signaling independently of DELLA factors is present in AMB-treated seeds.
source: These genetic observations suggest that a residual activity promoting ABA synthesis or signaling independently of DELLA factors is present in AMB-treated seeds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that AMB can still stimulate ABA-responsive gene expression in Δdella mutant seeds.

claim: Seeds that germinated in either presence of P. aeruginosa or AMB similarly produced pale seedlings whose growth was severely delayed bearing diminutive roots.
source: Seeds that germinated in either presence of P. aeruginosa or AMB similarly produced pale seedlings whose growth was severely delayed bearing diminutive roots (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Developmental defects diminished with increased distance between seeds and bacteria or decreased AMB concentrations.
source: These developmental defects diminished with increased distance between seeds and bacteria or decreased AMB concentrations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Developmental defects were no longer observed in seeds exposed to ∆ambE P. aeruginosa mutants, unable to produce AMB.
source: Furthermore, they were no longer observed in seeds exposed to ∆ambE P. aeruginosa mutants, unable to produce AMB (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: AMB released by P. aeruginosa severely perturbs seedling development.
source: Altogether, these observations show that AMB released by P. aeruginosa severely perturbs seedling development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of developmental defects in seedlings exposed to AMB.

claim: WT seeds that did not germinate germinated upon transfer to plates lacking P. aeruginosa and produced normal seedlings.
source: Remarkably, within a seed population exposed to P. aeruginosa, WT seeds that did not germinate germinated upon transfer to plates lacking P. aeruginosa and produced normal seedlings (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The resulting WT seedlings produced a normal seed yield.
source: The resulting WT seedlings produced a normal seed yield (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: WT seeds that had germinated in presence of P. aeruginosa failed to recover.
source: In contrast, WT seeds that had germinated in presence of P. aeruginosa failed to recover (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When WT and Δdella seeds were exposed for 3 days to P. aeruginosa prior to transfer to a bacteria-free medium, WT seeds had a higher survival rate relative to Δdella seeds.
source: Furthermore, when WT and Δdella seeds were exposed for 3 days to P. aeruginosa prior to transfer to a bacteria-free medium, WT seeds had a higher survival rate relative to Δdella seeds (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Germination-arrested seeds in presence of AMB are able to retain their vitality unlike newly emerged seedlings.
source: These observations therefore strongly suggest that germination-arrested seeds in presence of AMB are able to retain their vitality unlike newly emerged seedlings.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations that germination-arrested seeds can recover and produce normal plants.

claim: Oxyvinylglycines are known to inhibit irreversibly pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzymes.
source: Oxyvinylglycines are known to inhibit irreversibly pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzymes (Berkowitz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Berkowitz et al. (2006).

claim: AMB is a methionine analog.
source: Furthermore, AMB is a methionine analog.
evidence: This claim is based on the chemical structure of AMB.

claim: AMB does not block germination by interfering with ethylene, auxin or methionine synthesis.
source: Our results suggest that AMB does not block germination by interfering with ethylene, auxin or methionine synthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with ethylene, auxin, and methionine synthesis inhibitors and mutants.

claim: AMB interferes with an unknown and GA-independent mechanism promoting DELLA-dependent germination arrest.
source: Rather, our results indicate that AMB interferes with an unknown and GA-independent mechanism promoting DELLA-dependent germination arrest, which involves DELLA-dependent stimulation of ABA signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing GA-independent DELLA-dependent responses to AMB.

claim: 100 µM AVG inhibited the germination of Poa annua seeds.
source: Only in the case of AVG a GRA could be established using a pure synthetic compound: 100 µM AVG inhibited the germination of Poa annua seeds.
evidence: This claim is based on previous reports cited in the manuscript.

claim: As much as 200 µM AVG did not inhibit Arabidopsis seed germination, consistent with previous reports.
source: However, we found here that as much as 200 µM AVG did not inhibit Arabidopsis seed germination, consistent with previous reports (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation of previous work by Wilson et al. (2014).

claim: Dicot seeds are less responsive to P. fluorescens culture filtrates than graminaceous monocot seed.
source: Furthermore, dicot seeds are less responsive to P. fluorescens culture filtrates than graminaceous monocot seed, suggesting that FVG is less active to repress the germination of dicot seeds including seeds of cabbage, which is a brassicaceae (Banowetz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Banowetz et al. (2008).

claim: AMB-containing WT PAO1 extracts inhibited the germination of brassicaceae seeds, including cabbage seeds, unlike ∆ambE extracts.
source: We found that AMB-containing WT PAO1 extracts inhibited the germination of brassicaceae seeds, including cabbage seeds, unlike ∆ambE extracts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No such effect was observed with 250 µM AVG.
source: No such effect was observed with 250 µM AVG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oxyvinylglycines do not affect seed germination in the same manner.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that oxyvinylglycines do not affect seed germination in the same manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of effects of different oxyvinylglycines on seed germination.

claim: AMB is an oxyvinylglycine able to repress the germination of several seed dicot species.
source: They also strongly suggest that AMB is an oxyvinylglycine able to repress the germination of several seed dicot species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with brassicaceae seeds.

claim: Brassicaceae seeds that germinated in presence of WT PAO1 extracts developed developmental defects unlike those germinated in presence of ∆ambE extracts.
source: Furthermore, brassicaceae seeds that germinated in presence of WT PAO1 extracts developed developmental defects unlike those germinated in presence of ∆ambE extracts (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Germination arrested Capsella seeds in presence of WT PAO1 extracts were protected as they produced normal seedlings upon transfer to a normal medium.
source: Germination arrested Capsella seeds in presence of WT PAO1 extracts were protected as they produced normal seedlings upon transfer to a normal medium (Figure 7—figure supplement 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3E and F.

claim: AVG is a well-known inhibitor of 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC) synthase.
source: AVG is a well-known inhibitor of 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC) synthase, a PLP-dependent enzyme catalyzing the synthesis of ACC, a precursor of ethylene, from S-adenosylmethionine (Adams and Yang, 1979; Huai et al., 2001; Capitani et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Adams and Yang (1979), Huai et al. (2001), and Capitani et al. (2002).

claim: AVG was also shown to inhibit auxin synthesis.
source: AVG was also shown to inhibit auxin synthesis (Soeno et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Soeno et al. (2010).

claim: AMB may also inhibit ACC synthase as suggested by a report showing that AMB decreases ethylene levels in apples.
source: AMB may also inhibit ACC synthase as suggested by a report showing that AMB decreases ethylene levels in apples; however, whether AMB can inhibit ACC synthase in vitro was not shown (Mattoo et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on citation of previous work by Mattoo et al. (1979).

claim: 5 µM AVG lowers ethylene synthesis in Arabidopsis seeds and does not inhibit germination.
source: Wilson et al. previously reported that 5 µM AVG, a widely used inhibitor of ACC synthase, lowers ethylene synthesis in Arabidopsis seeds and does not inhibit germination (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Wilson et al. (2014).

claim: Heptuple acs mutant seeds, deficient several in ACS biosynthetic genes, germinated similarly to WT seeds.
source: Furthermore, heptuple acs mutant seeds, deficient several in ACS biosynthetic genes, germinated similarly to WT seeds (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Seeds treated with silver nitrate (AgNO3), which induces ethylene insensitivity, did not show an inhibition of seed germination.
source: We also treated seeds with silver nitrate (AgNO3), which induces ethylene insensitivity, and did not observe an inhibition of seed germination (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C) (Rodríguez et al., 1999; McDaniel and Binder, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C and citation of previous work.

claim: Inhibition of ethylene biosynthesis upon seed imbibition is not sufficient to block germination.
source: Altogether, these experiments show that inhibition of ethylene biosynthesis upon seed imbibition is not sufficient to block germination and therefore are not consistent with the hypothesis that AMB blocks germination because it blocks ethylene biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with ethylene synthesis inhibitors and mutants.

claim: AMB could also inhibit methionyl-transfer RNA synthetase indicating that it could act as a methionine antimetabolite.
source: AMB could also inhibit methionyl-transfer RNA synthetase indicating that it could act as a methionine antimetabolite (Mattoo et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Mattoo et al. (1979).

claim: The effect of AMB to block germination resulting from its inhibition of auxin synthesis is unlikely because auxin promotes ABA-dependent repression of seed germination.
source: This could suggest that the effect of AMB to block germination results from its inhibition of auxin or methionine synthesis. The former possibility is unlikely because (1) auxin promotes ABA-dependent repression of seed germination and (2) low auxin levels may facilitate seed germination since ABA-dependent inhibition of radicle elongations involves enhancement of auxin signaling in the radicle elongation zone (Belin et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is inferred from previous knowledge about auxin's role in seed germination and supported by citation of previous work by Belin et al. (2009) and Liu et al. (2013).

claim: tir1 mutants, deficient in the auxin receptor TIR1, germinate normally.
source: We found that tir1 mutants, deficient in the auxin receptor TIR1, germinate normally, consistent with the report of Liu et al. showing that tir1/afb2 and tir1/afb3 double mutants, deficient in the auxin receptors TIR1 and AFB1 or TIR1 and AFB3, germinate normally and are less dormant (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and B, Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and B and citation of previous work by Liu et al. (2013).

claim: WT seeds treated with 500 µM of yucasin, a potent inhibitor of the YUCCA proteins, did not prevent their germination.
source: Furthermore, WT seeds treated with 500 µM of yucasin, a potent inhibitor of the YUCCA proteins, which are flavin mono-oxygenases oxidizing indole-3–pyruvic acid to indole-3–acetic acid (auxin), did not prevent their germination (Figure 7—figure supplement 5C) (Nishimura et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5C and citation of previous work by Nishimura et al. (2014).

claim: Low auxin signaling or synthesis upon seed imbibition does not prevent seed germination.
source: These data indicate that low auxin signaling or synthesis upon seed imbibition does not prevent seed germination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with auxin synthesis inhibitors and mutants.

claim: tir1 mutant seed germination responses to AMB-containing WT PAO1 extracts was similar to that of WT seeds.
source: In addition, tir1 mutant seed germination responses to AMB-containing WT PAO1 extracts was similar to that of WT seeds, indicating that AMB-dependent responses in seeds do not require auxin signaling (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Methionine biosynthesis is essential for seed germination.
source: Concerning methionine, previous reports showed that methionine biosynthesis is essential for seed germination (Gallardo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Gallardo et al. (2002).

claim: DL-Propargylgylcine (PAG) is an active site-directed inhibitor of cystathionine γ-synthase, which is necessary for methionine synthesis.
source: DL-Propargylgylcine (PAG) is an active site-directed inhibitor of cystathionine γ-synthase, which is necessary for methionine synthesis (Thompson et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Thompson et al. (1982).

claim: WT seeds treated with 1 mM PAG were unable to germinate.
source: WT seeds treated with 1 mM PAG were unable to germinate, consistent with previous reports (Gallardo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation of previous work by Gallardo et al. (2002).

claim: Exogenously added methionine in the germination medium fully restored germination in PAG-treated seeds.
source: As expected and consistent with previous reports, exogenously added methionine in the germination medium fully restored germination in PAG-treated seeds (Figure 7—figure supplement 6) (Gallardo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6 and citation of previous work by Gallardo et al. (2002).

claim: Exogenous methionine did not rescue the germination of PAO1 treated WT seeds.
source: However, exogenous methionine did not rescue the germination of PAO1 treated WT seeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: These observations are not consistent with the hypothesis that AMB prevents germination by limiting methionine synthesis.
source: These observations are not consistent with the hypothesis that AMB prevents germination by limiting methionine synthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results with methionine supplementation.

claim: The mechanism through which AMB enhances DELLA activity to promote ABA-dependent responses in seeds remains to be understood.
source: The mechanism through which AMB enhances DELLA activity to promote ABA-dependent responses in seeds remains to be understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Whether AMB enhances DELLA activity through a direct interaction between AMB and DELLAs is not known.
source: In particular, whether it is the result of a direct interaction between AMB and DELLAs is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: 87 genes whose expression is regulated by DELLA factors in seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts were identified.
source: In this respect, our transcriptome analysis identified 87 genes whose expression is regulated by DELLA factors in seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa extracts (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Among the 87 genes, 24 genes had their expression unchanged when GA was included in the medium together with P. aeruginosa extracts.
source: Among them, 24 genes had their expression unchanged when GA was included in the medium together with P. aeruginosa extracts (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3D and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The expression of 18 of the 24 genes was not significantly changed in seeds exposed to paclobutrazol (PAC).
source: Interestingly, the expression of 18 of them was not significantly changed in seeds exposed to paclobutrazol (PAC), an inhibitor of GA synthesis, further suggesting these genes are not regulated by GA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: In the set of 18 genes, those related to karrikin signaling were overrepresented.
source: In this set of genes, those related to karrikin signaling were overrepresented (Nelson et al., 2009; Waters et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq analysis and supported by citation of previous work by Nelson et al. (2009) and Waters et al. (2012).

claim: Karrikins are a class of compounds found in the smoke of burning plant material, which are known to promote germination and to break seed dormancy.
source: Karrikins are a class of compounds found in the smoke of burning plant material, which are known to promote germination and to break seed dormancy (Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Nelson et al. (2009).

claim: Seeds lacking the karrikin receptor KAI2 are dormant.
source: Furthermore, seeds lacking the karrikin receptor KAI2 are dormant (Waters et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Waters et al. (2012).

claim: The karrikin signaling genes KUF1 and BBX20/STH7 are strongly repressed in WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa but not in Δdella mutant seeds.
source: The karrikin signaling genes KUF1 and BBX20/STH7 are strongly repressed in WT seeds exposed to P. aeruginosa but not in Δdella mutant seeds, lacking all DELLA factors (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: AMB could repress germination by repressing karrikin signaling through the DELLAs.
source: Thus, our data suggest that AMB could repress germination by repressing karrikin signaling through the DELLAs.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: Karrikins share common signaling components with strigolactones, a class of plant hormones also promoting germination.
source: However, karrikins share common signaling components with strigolactones, a class of plant hormones also promoting germination (De Cuyper et al., 2017; Toh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by De Cuyper et al. (2017) and Toh et al. (2012).

claim: Strigolactones were recently proposed to regulate GA signaling in rice.
source: Strigolactones were recently proposed to regulate GA signaling in rice (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Ito et al. (2017).

claim: SLR1, a rice DELLA factor, was found to interact with the strigolactone receptor DWARF14 fused to its ligand.
source: SLR1, a rice DELLA factor, was found to interact with the strigolactone receptor DWARF14 fused to its ligand (Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Nakamura et al. (2013).

claim: AMB could also potentially regulate strigolactone signaling in seeds.
source: Thus, AMB could also potentially regulate strigolactone signaling in seeds.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the discussion of karrikin and strigolactone signaling.

claim: IQS is the autoinducer of the recently discovered quorum sensing (QS) subsystem named IQS in P. aeruginosa, controlled by the five-gene operon ambABCDE.
source: Indeed, genetic experiments have shown that IQS, the autoinducer of the recently discovered quorum sensing (QS) subsystem named IQS in P. aeruginosa, is controlled by the five-gene operon ambABCDE (Lee et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Lee et al. (2013a).

claim: The link between ambABCDE and IQS synthesis remains to be determined.
source: Although the IQS receptor remains unknown it also remains to be determined what is the link between ambABCDE and IQS synthesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Lee et al. first proposed that ambABCDE gene products are directly responsible for IQS synthesis and therefore activity of the quorum sensing IQS.
source: Indeed, Lee et al. first proposed that ambABCDE gene products are directly responsible for IQS synthesis and therefore activity of the quorum sensing IQS (Lee et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Lee et al. (2013a).

claim: Lee et al. showed that ambABCDE is also necessary for AMB production.
source: However, the link between ambABCDE and IQS synthesis remains to be clarified. Indeed Lee et al. showed that ambABCDE is also necessary for AMB production and Rojas Murcia et al. proposed that ambABCDE gene products rather synthesize and export AMB (Rojas Murcia et al., 2015; reviewed in Moradali et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010b, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Lee et al. (2010b, 2013a).

claim: Rojas Murcia et al. proposed that ambABCDE gene products rather synthesize and export AMB.
source: Indeed Lee et al. showed that ambABCDE is also necessary for AMB production and Rojas Murcia et al. proposed that ambABCDE gene products rather synthesize and export AMB (Rojas Murcia et al., 2015; reviewed in Moradali et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010b, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Rojas Murcia et al. (2015).

claim: Presence of the ambABCDE operon is necessary for IQS production and signaling.
source: In any case, there is no genetic controversy regarding the need of a functional ambABCDE operon for (1) IQS production and signaling and (2) AMB synthesis and release by P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is based on the cited literature.

claim: Presence of the ambABCDE operon is necessary for AMB synthesis and release by P. aeruginosa.
source: In any case, there is no genetic controversy regarding the need of a functional ambABCDE operon for (1) IQS production and signaling and (2) AMB synthesis and release by P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is based on the cited literature and experimental data in this study.

claim: AMB is abolished in ΔlasIΔrhlI P. aeruginosa mutants lacking the las and rhl QS subsystems.
source: Furthermore, we show that AMB is also abolished in ΔlasIΔrhlI P. aeruginosa mutants lacking the las and rhl QS subsystems (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Expression of amb operon is strongly downregulated in ΔlasIΔrhlI mutants.
source: This is in agreement with a previous report showing that expression of amb operon is strongly downregulated in ΔlasIΔrhlI mutants (Schuster et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Schuster et al. (2003).

claim: The genes of the ambABCDE operon were singled out as quorum-dependent genes in chronic cystic fibrosis patients infected with P. aeruginosa.
source: The genes of the ambABCDE operon were also singled out as quorum-dependent genes in chronic cystic fibrosis patients infected with P. aeruginosa (Chugani et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Chugani et al. (2012).

claim: The ambABCDE operon, which is necessary for AMB production, is being intimately linked to the activity of QS in P. aeruginosa.
source: Thus, these reports leave little doubt that the ambABCDE operon, which is necessary for AMB production, is being intimately linked to the activity of QS in P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited literature and experimental data.

claim: The ambABCDE operon is present in numerous P. aeruginosa strains.
source: Publicly available genomic sequences show that the ambABCDE operon is not only present in the P. aeruginosa PAO1 strain used in this study but is also present in numerous other P. aeruginosa strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 11.

claim: Arabidopsis produces high seed numbers.
source: Arabidopsis produces high seed numbers, which could contradict the need of evolving protective germination arrest responses since one successful germination event is sufficient to maintain the size of the population.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about Arabidopsis.

claim: Arabidopsis is not a long distance seed dispersal species and the majority of seeds is expected to fall in the vicinity of the mother plant.
source: However, Arabidopsis is not a long distance seed dispersal species and the majority of seeds is expected to fall in the vicinity of the mother plant.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about Arabidopsis.

claim: Arabidopsis seedlings are small and fragile and poor dispersion would increase their chance of being killed at the same time whenever faced by a local threat.
source: Furthermore, Arabidopsis seedlings are small and fragile and poor dispersion would increase their chance of being killed at the same time whenever faced by a local threat.
evidence: This is inferred from general knowledge about Arabidopsis.

claim: Arabidopsis has evolved elaborate germination arrest control mechanisms that are widely regarded as being protective.
source: It is therefore expected that early development is tightly regulated in Arabidopsis to enhance plant survival. Indeed, Arabidopsis has evolved elaborate germination arrest control mechanisms that are widely regarded as being protective.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about Arabidopsis seed germination control.

claim: Seed dormancy is believed to prevent germination out of season.
source: These include seed dormancy, believed to prevent germination out of season, and control of seed germination of non-dormant seeds in response to abiotic factors, which is also considered to protect the plant (Kami et al., 2010; Penfield and King, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Kami et al. (2010) and Penfield and King (2009).

claim: Control of seed germination of non-dormant seeds in response to abiotic factors is considered to protect the plant.
source: These include seed dormancy, believed to prevent germination out of season, and control of seed germination of non-dormant seeds in response to abiotic factors, which is also considered to protect the plant (Kami et al., 2010; Penfield and King, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Kami et al. (2010) and Penfield and King (2009).

claim: Laboratory conditions were described where the AMB-dependent germination arrest protects the plant from the potentially fatal effect of AMB on seedlings.
source: Here, we described laboratory conditions where the AMB-dependent germination arrest protects the plant from the potentially fatal effect of AMB on seedlings (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The AMB-dependent germination arrest could indicate that this response has evolved as an adaption to counteract damage induced by biotic harmful compounds.
source: This could indicate that this response has evolved as an adaption to counteract damage induced by biotic harmful compounds similarly to what is proposed for abiotic stresses.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The AMB-dependent germination arrest could correspond to a protection mechanism against pathogenic bacteria in the environment.
source: More generally, it is also consistent with the notion that it could correspond to a protection mechanism against pathogenic bacteria in the environment.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Given the link between AMB and QS activity in P. aeruginosa, evolving a germination arrest response to AMB could be doubly advantageous: it could protect the plant from the AMB toxin and it could reveal the presence of the plant pathogen P. aeruginosa.
source: Given the link between AMB and QS activity in P. aeruginosa, it is tempting to speculate that evolving a germination arrest response to AMB could be doubly advantageous: (1) it could protect the plant from the AMB toxin and (2) it could reveal the presence of the plant pathogen P. aeruginosa.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the experimental observations and the link between AMB and QS.

claim: The GRAs released by P. aeruginosa are observed after culturing P. aeruginosa to high densities that trigger IQS QS activity.
source: Indeed, the GRAs released by P. aeruginosa reported here are observed after culturing P. aeruginosa to high densities that trigger IQS QS activity.
evidence: This is based on the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Whether bacteria such as P. aeruginosa proliferate to such high densities in the rhizosphere is unclear.
source: Whether bacteria such as P. aeruginosa proliferate to such high densities in the rhizosphere is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Green et al. were able to detect P. aeruginosa in 24% of soil samples studied and reported that it multiplied in lettuce and bean under conditions of high temperature and high humidity.
source: Green et al. were able to detect P. aeruginosa in 24% of soil samples studied and reported that it multiplied in lettuce and bean under conditions of high temperature and high humidity (Green et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Green et al. (1974).

claim: Deredjian et al. reported that P. aeruginosa has low occurrence in agricultural soils.
source: On the other hand, Deredjian et al. reported that P. aeruginosa has low occurrence in agricultural soils.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Deredjian et al. (2014).

claim: Deredjian et al. were able to detect P. aeruginosa in high amounts in various manures.
source: However, they were able to detect them in high amounts in various manures, consistent with previous reports (Deredjian et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Deredjian et al. (2014).

claim: P. aeruginosa could only be found in high densities in the rhizosphere where food is available, including near decaying fruit or animal droppings, together with the proper moisture or temperature conditions.
source: These results could suggest that P. aeruginosa could only be found in high densities in the rhizosphere where food is available, including near decaying fruit or animal droppings, together with the proper moisture or temperature conditions.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the cited literature.

claim: High densities of bacteria in the rhizosphere may not be obligatory to elicit seed germination responses.
source: On the other hand, high densities of bacteria in the rhizosphere may not be obligatory to elicit seed germination responses.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on reasoning about quorum sensing.

claim: A given individual bacterium can only detect the autoinducer concentration present in its immediate proximity, which can include the autoinducer molecules that the same bacterium releases.
source: The Quorum Sensing is usually invoked to describe situations when high densities of cells trigger coordinated responses after autoinducers reach high concentrations in the environment. However, a given individual bacterium can only detect the autoinducer concentration present in its immediate proximity, which can include the autoinducer molecules that the same bacterium releases.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about quorum sensing.

claim: In the rhizosphere, there could be situations limiting autoinducer diffusion, altering autoinducer advection, reducing autoinducer degradation or altering autoinducer spatial distribution, which could lead to high local concentrations of autoinducer even in absence of high densities of bacteria.
source: In the rhizosphere, there could be situations limiting autoinducer diffusion, altering autoinducer advection, reducing autoinducer degradation or altering autoinducer spatial distribution, which could lead to high local concentrations of autoinducer even in absence of high densities of bacteria.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on reasoning about quorum sensing in the rhizosphere.

claim: Autoinducers fulfill a role beyond that of detecting high densities of bacteria.
source: Thus, a given bacteria cannot distinguish among the various scenarios leading to high autoinducer concentration. These considerations lead to the proposal that autoinducers fulfill a role beyond that of detecting high densities of bacteria (Redfield, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Redfield (2002).

claim: Autoinducers could allow bacteria to sense whether diffusion of molecules in their immediate environment is limited (Diffusion Sensing –DS-).
source: They could allow bacteria to sense whether diffusion of molecules in their immediate environment is limited (Diffusion Sensing –DS-).
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about quorum sensing and supported by citation of Hense et al. (2007).

claim: Diffusion sensing would allow a given bacteria to determine whether a given effector would diffuse efficiently or not.
source: In turn, this would allow a given bacteria to determine whether a given effector would diffuse efficiently or not (Hense et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation of previous work by Hense et al. (2007).
